segments.text: How does an AI model learn that Jelly fits after peanut butter end before a user ever prompts it?
It learns from examples.
To understand how, we have to separate the user interface from the technology underneath.
Chat GPT is the app. The LLM is the engine.
Under the hood, a large language model, or LLM, does the work.
The large part of that engine refers to scale.
These models are trained by processing massive amounts of text and computer code,
language describes the model's core functions,
reading, writing, summarizing, translating, and explaining information.
Finally, a model uses learned numerical patterns to predict a likely output.
To see where those patterns come from, we have to look at the training process.
It starts with step one, read.
The training process takes an example where the correct answer is already included in the text.
In step two, the model makes a guess.
Given the words peanut butter and, it tries to predict what comes next.
In this instance, the model guesses cloud.
It makes this error because it is calculating a prediction rather than looking up a fact.
That leads to step three, check.
The model compares that incorrect guess against the word Jelly, which actually appears in the example.
Finally, in step four, the model adjusts.
It changes its internal numbers to shift the probability of its future answers.
This adjustment ensures that Jelly becomes a more likely mathematical output
the next time the model encounters this specific situation.
One correction doesn't teach the model everything.
The process requires constant repetition.
The model repeats this read, guess, check, adjust cycle across billions of different examples.
After billions of these training cycles, the final result is a set of learned patterns.
After peanut butter and, Jelly is a familiar continuation.
Twinkle, twinkle, little, star, once upon a, time, better late then, never.
Simple phrases like these make the concept visible, but the learning reaches much further into complex structures.
The model identifies patterns in how people explain ideas, solve logical problems, and even how they misspell words.
Training has built patterns into the model's internal numbers.
Now let's see how the model uses those patterns to build an answer.
Suppose you type, I'd like to buy peanut butter and…
The model uses the patterns that learn during training to calculate what might come next.
It doesn't retrieve a fully formed answer from a pre-written database.
Instead, it builds the response from scratch, one piece at a time.
For visual simplicity in this lesson, we will look at whole words,
but in reality, models generate tokens, which can be full words or just fragments of words.
Based on its training, the model calculates a 41% chance the next word is Jelly.
It gives bread 27%, bananas 16%, and honey 5%.
Keep in mind, these percentages are illustrative examples to show how the concept works.
The remaining probability is split among all other possible words to reach 100%.
While Jelly has the highest probability here, it is not a forced choice.
Now watch what happens when we change the text slightly.
On the right, the sentence reads,
I'd like to buy a peanut butter and banana.
The new percentages reflect this updated context.
Sandwich gets 54%, smoothie 16%, toast 9%, and Jelly drops to only 2%.
The surrounding words dictate these odds.
That specific context causes Jelly to plummet from a 41% chance down to just 2%.
This diagram shows a process similar to the predictive text keyboard on your phone.
It suggests a word, you tap it, and it suggests the next.
But a language model continuously loops this action automatically to build a complete answer.
Looking at the first panel, we start the loop with,
I want to buy peanut butter and the model calculates the probabilities and adds the word Jelly.
In the second step, the text now says, I want to buy peanut butter and Jelly.
The model uses that entire updated string to calculate the next step, adding the word 4.
Moving to the third panel, the context expands to, and Jelly 4.
Based on this new input, the model adds lunch.
The foundational rule is that each chosen word immediately becomes part of the input for the
very next prediction.
To generate a full paragraph, the model runs this exact loop of predicting, adding, and updating
many times over.
It happens at speeds fast enough to look like active thought.
Training builds the patterns.
The model uses those patterns to build your answer.
One word at a time.
